{{Short description|Knot that can't be tied in a string of constant diameter}}
[[Image:Wild knot.svg|thumb|400px|A wild knot]]

In the [[knot theory|mathematical theory of knots]], a knot is '''tame''' if it can be "thickened", that is, if there exists an extension to an [[embedding]] of the [[solid torus]] <math>S^1\times D^2</math> into the [[3-sphere]]. A knot is tame if and only if it can be represented as a finite [[polygonal chain|closed polygonal chain]]. In knot theory and [[3-manifold]] theory, often the adjective "tame" is omitted. Smooth knots, for example, are always tame.

Knots that are not tame are called '''wild''' and can have [[pathological (mathematics)|pathological]] behavior.
Every closed curve containing a [[wild arc]] is a wild knot.<ref>{{SpringerEOM|title=Wild knot|first=M. I.|last=Voitsekhovskii|mode=cs2|date=December 13, 2014|oldid=35622}}</ref>
It has been conjectured that every '''wild knot''' has infinitely many [[quadrisecant]]s.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Kuperberg | first = Greg | author-link = Greg Kuperberg
 | arxiv = math/9712205
 | doi = 10.1142/S021821659400006X
 | journal = [[Journal of Knot Theory and Its Ramifications]]
 | mr = 1265452
 | pages = 41–50
 | title = Quadrisecants of knots and links
 | volume = 3
 | year = 1994| s2cid = 6103528 }}</ref>

As well as their mathematical study, wild knots have also been studied for their potential for decorative purposes in [[Celtic knot|Celtic-style]] [[List of decorative knots|ornamental knotwork]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Browne | first = Cameron
 | date = December 2006
 | doi = 10.1016/j.cag.2006.08.021
 | issue = 6
 | journal = Computers & Graphics
 | pages = 1027–1032
 | title = Wild knots
 | volume = 30}}</ref>
